title: Feasibility and safety of cellular therapy for in-utero repair of myelomeningocele (CuRe Trial): a first-in-human, phase 1, single-arm study
summary: Surgeons at UC Davis applied allogeneic human placenta-derived mesenchymal stem cells directly onto the exposed spinal cord during standard fetal surgery for six fetuses with severe spina bifida (myelomeningocele). All six children were born with intact repairs, no cell-related adverse effects, and reversal of the hindbrain herniation typically associated with the condition. It is the first time a live cellular therapy has been delivered in utero, and the results support advancing to a larger phase 1/2a cohort.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and thelancet.com: no retractions, corrections, or PubPeer threads found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Randomized phase 2b dose-escalation trial of stem cell therapy with laromestrocel for aging frailty
summary: In a 148-person randomized trial, a single IV infusion of allogeneic bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (laromestrocel) produced dose- and time-dependent gains in 6-minute-walk distance versus placebo in adults aged 70-85 with clinical frailty, with the largest doses adding roughly 63 meters at 9 months. It is among the largest controlled trials to date testing an off-the-shelf allogeneic cell therapy against a hallmark of biological aging rather than a single disease.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and cell.com: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24. Note: the independent commentary site 'The Niche' (Paul Knoepfler, March 2026) raised methodological questions about an unexplained decline in the placebo group's walk-test scores between months 3 and 9, and criticized overselling in accompanying press coverage -- this is post-publication commentary, not a peer-reviewed correction.

title: Stem-Cell-Derived Biologic Ventricular Assist Tissue in Heart Failure
summary: In the ongoing BioVAT-HF trial, 20 patients with advanced heart failure received an implanted patch of induced-pluripotent-stem-cell-derived engineered heart muscle sewn onto the epicardium. At 3 months the grafts thickened the treated heart wall by 4.5 mm and improved ejection fraction and quality-of-life scores, with benefits partly sustained out to 36 months in long-term follow-up. It is one of the first controlled trials showing an iPSC-derived tissue graft can measurably remuscularize a failing human heart.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nejm.org: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Daraxonrasib or Chemotherapy in Previously Treated Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer
summary: The phase 3 RASolute 302 trial randomized patients with previously treated metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to daraxonrasib, an oral pan-RAS(ON) inhibitor, or standard chemotherapy. Daraxonrasib nearly doubled median overall survival (13.2 vs 6.7 months, hazard ratio 0.40) along with improved progression-free survival, a magnitude of benefit described by investigators as unprecedented for this cancer. Dermatologic toxicity and emerging resistance via KRAS amplification and other pathway alterations remain open challenges.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nejm.org: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour
summary: The International Brain Laboratory, a 12-lab consortium, recorded from more than 600,000 neurons across 279 brain regions in 139 mice performing a decision-making task, producing the first standardized, brain-wide activity atlas of its kind. Task-related and movement-related signals were found to be far more broadly distributed across the brain than prior single-region studies suggested. The underlying dataset and pipeline are openly released, and the finding has already reshaped how the field designs region-specific versus brain-wide circuit studies.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nature.com: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Genome modelling and design across all domains of life with Evo 2
summary: Evo 2 is a 40-billion-parameter DNA foundation model trained on over 9 trillion nucleotides spanning all domains of life, capable of predicting variant effects and generating synthetic genomic sequences from DNA to RNA to protein. Arc Institute and collaborators showed it can classify pathogenic mutations zero-shot and design functional genetic elements without task-specific fine-tuning. It has become one of the most widely used open genomic foundation models since its 2025 preprint release, though independent benchmarks have since identified specific blind spots.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nature.com: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Restoring rapid natural bimanual typing with a neuroprosthesis after paralysis
summary: BrainGate investigators built an intracortical brain-computer interface that decodes attempted finger movements on a QWERTY layout, letting two participants -- one with ALS, one with a cervical spinal cord injury -- type at up to 22 words per minute with a 1.6% word error rate, approaching able-bodied typing accuracy. This is a substantial throughput jump over prior hand-motor intracortical BCI decoders and moves implanted typing interfaces closer to practical, everyday communication for people with paralysis.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nature.com: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Patient-Specific In Vivo Gene Editing to Treat a Rare Genetic Disease
summary: A CHOP/Penn team designed, manufactured, and administered a bespoke in vivo CRISPR base-editing therapy for an infant ("KJ") with life-threatening carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1) deficiency in under six months, using lipid nanoparticles to deliver a base editor targeted to his specific mutation. After two infusions the child tolerated substantially more dietary protein and a lower dose of nitrogen-scavenger medication with no serious adverse events. It is the first published case of a fully individualized, patient-specific gene-editing drug, though it is a single-patient case study and experts have flagged open questions about manufacturing scalability and regulatory pathways for replicating the approach.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and nejm.org: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Vascular network-inspired diffusible scaffolds for engineering functional midbrain organoids
summary: Standard neural organoids suffer necrotic, hypoxic cores because nutrients and oxygen can only diffuse in from the surface. This group 3D-printed vascular-network-inspired diffusible (VID) scaffolds -- meshed tubular channel networks -- into culture wells, letting midbrain organoids grow with far less necrosis and hypoxia, along with better dopaminergic neuron maturation, more complex network activity, and more physiologically realistic drug responses. It's a low-tech, broadly adoptable alternative to microfluidic or vascularized-implant approaches for solving organoid diffusion limits.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and cell.com: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Distinct in vivo dynamics of donor-derived stem cell memory CAR T cells post-allogeneic HSCT relapse
summary: Researchers co-led by Luca Gattinoni and James Kochenderfer engineered CAR T cells that acquire a stem-cell-memory (TSCM) phenotype and tested them in a first-in-human trial in patients relapsing after allogeneic stem cell transplant. The TSCM-phenotype CAR T cells expanded and persisted markedly better than conventional CAR T products, driving complete responses at doses as low as 250,000 cells/kg without lymphodepleting chemotherapy beforehand. Lower effective doses and no chemo preconditioning could translate into a substantially safer, less toxic CAR-T regimen if the results hold up in larger cohorts.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and cell.com: no retractions or corrections found as of 2026-07-24.

title: Human embryonic stem cell-derived dopaminergic cells for Parkinson's disease: a phase 1/2 open-label trial
summary: In this first-in-human European trial, researchers transplanted dopamine-producing neurons grown from human embryonic stem cells directly into the brains of eight people with moderate Parkinson's disease. After 12 months of follow-up under immunosuppression, the cell product caused no serious product-related adverse events and no graft-induced dyskinesia, a major feasibility milestone for replacing the neurons lost in Parkinson's disease with lab-grown cells. One of eight participants died from an unrelated pulmonary infection during follow-up, not attributed to the cell product. The trial is among the first pluripotent stem-cell therapies for Parkinson's approved for clinical testing in Europe.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the Nature Medicine site directly on 2026-07-25: no retraction, correction, or expression of concern found.

title: Enhancer-directed gene delivery for digit regeneration based on conserved epidermal factors
summary: Comparing regenerating zebrafish fins, salamander limbs, and mouse digit tips, researchers found that the transcription factors SP6 and SP8 act as a conserved genetic switch in wound skin that drives appendage regrowth, and that removing them blocks bony digit-tip regeneration in mice. They then packaged an AAV gene therapy carrying a zebrafish-derived regeneration enhancer to deliver FGF8, a downstream SP target, directly to amputation wounds, partially restoring regeneration in SP-deficient mice and accelerating it in normal mice. It is an early proof-of-concept for injury-site-specific gene therapy that could one day help regrow lost digit or limb tissue.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the PNAS site directly on 2026-07-25: no retraction or correction found.

title: Physiology and immunology of a pig-to-human decedent kidney xenotransplant
summary: Surgeons transplanted a minimally gene-edited pig kidney into a brain-dead human maintained on a ventilator for a pre-planned 61-day study, the longest such xenotransplant physiology study to date. The kidney sustained hemodynamic and electrolyte stability and dialysis independence for weeks; antibody-mediated rejection emerged around day 33 but was fully reversed with plasma exchange, complement inhibition, and anti-thymocyte globulin. The study demonstrates both the promise and the immunological hurdles of pig-to-human kidney xenotransplantation as a potential answer to the organ-donor shortage.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and Nature's site on 2026-07-25: no retraction found. Note a Publisher Correction (2026-02-12) and an Author Correction (2026-06-04) fixing mislabeled cell-frequency percentages in an extended data figure (e.g. a value corrected from '48%' to '0.48%'); these are figure-data corrections that do not affect the paper's core conclusions.

title: Sacituzumab Govitecan plus Pembrolizumab for Advanced Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
summary: This international phase 3 trial (443 patients across 186 sites in 28 countries) tested whether adding the antibody-drug conjugate sacituzumab govitecan to the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab works better than standard chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab as first-line treatment for PD-L1-positive metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. The combination cut the risk of progression or death by 35% (median progression-free survival 11.2 vs. 7.8 months) with a higher response rate and fewer treatment discontinuations. The FDA approved the combination in June 2026 based on these results, making it a likely new standard of care for this aggressive cancer subtype.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the NEJM site directly on 2026-07-25: no retraction or correction found.

title: Efficacy and safety of oral semaglutide 14 mg (flexible dose) in early-stage symptomatic Alzheimer's disease (evoke and evoke+): two phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trials
summary: Two identically designed phase 3 trials tested whether once-daily oral semaglutide (the active ingredient in Ozempic/Wegovy) could slow Alzheimer's progression in 3,808 adults with amyloid-confirmed early-stage disease, followed for up to 156 weeks across 566 sites in 40 countries. Despite strong hope from observational and diabetes-trial data suggesting GLP-1 drugs protect the brain, semaglutide showed no benefit over placebo on cognitive or functional decline, though it did significantly lower CSF biomarkers of tau pathology and neuroinflammation. The dissociation between biomarker activity and clinical benefit is a high-profile negative result for one of the most-hyped drug classes in medicine.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the Lancet site directly on 2026-07-25: no retraction or correction found.

title: Neuroproteasomes regulate endogenous tau paired helical filament formation in an APOE genotype- and age-dependent manner
summary: Researchers discovered that neurons have a specialized proteasome embedded in their plasma membrane, dubbed a 'neuroproteasome', that normally keeps the Alzheimer's-linked protein tau from misfolding. Using a novel cell-impermeant inhibitor, they showed that blocking this neuroproteasome rapidly causes normal tau to misfold into paired helical filaments, the same structures found in Alzheimer's brains. The APOE4 gene variant, the strongest genetic Alzheimer's risk factor, reduces neuroproteasome levels at the membrane by about a third, while the protective APOE2 variant nearly doubles them, offering a mechanistic bridge between genetic risk, aging, and the onset of tau pathology.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the Nature Neuroscience site directly on 2026-07-25: no retraction, correction, or expression of concern found.

title: Advancing regulatory variant effect prediction with AlphaGenome
summary: DeepMind's AlphaGenome is a unified deep-learning model that reads up to one million base pairs of DNA and predicts thousands of molecular readouts, including gene expression, chromatin accessibility, histone marks, transcription-factor binding, 3D chromatin contacts, and splicing, at single-base resolution. It matches or beats specialized state-of-the-art models in 25 of 26 variant-effect benchmarks, and the authors show it can simultaneously explain multiple mechanisms behind clinically relevant mutations near the TAL1 oncogene. It is a discriminative regulatory-genomics model, distinct from generative sequence-design models such as Evo 2.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the Nature site directly on 2026-07-25: no retraction or correction found.

title: A neuroprosthesis for restoring hand movement and sensation in a person with complete tetraplegia
summary: Researchers built a 'double neural bypass', a hybrid brain-computer interface that reads intracortical signals related to movement intent and uses AI to drive electrical stimulation of the spinal cord and forearm muscles, restoring real-time hand grasp in a man with complete C4/C5 tetraplegia. Sensors on a hand orthosis simultaneously feed pressure data back into the sensory cortex via intracortical microstimulation, restoring a sense of touch. Over three years, the participant regained the ability to self-feed and grasp objects, with lasting gains in arm strength and tactile sensitivity even when the device was switched off, suggesting the system induced genuine neuroplasticity years after his injury.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the Nature Medicine site directly on 2026-07-25: no retraction, correction, or expression of concern found.

title: Human microphysiological systems of aging recreate the in vivo process expediting evaluation of anti-geronic strategies
summary: Bioengineers built a human iPSC-derived organ-on-chip system linking engineered white-adipose and liver tissue, then perfused it with blood serum from older versus younger human donors. Within four days, serum from older donors induced chronic inflammation, impaired glucose regulation, disrupted fat metabolism, and cellular senescence, hallmarks that normally take decades to develop in people, while young serum reversed some of these changes. The system is proposed as a fast, human-relevant platform for testing anti-aging interventions without waiting years for results.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the Nature Biomedical Engineering site directly on 2026-07-25: no retraction, correction, or expression of concern found.

title: Prime Editing for p47phox-Deficient Chronic Granulomatous Disease
summary: This paper reports the first peer-reviewed clinical use of prime editing, a 'search-and-replace' gene-editing technology that corrects mutations without cutting both DNA strands, in human patients. Two patients with p47phox-deficient chronic granulomatous disease, a severe inherited immune disorder, received an infusion of their own blood stem cells corrected with the prime editor PM359. Both patients showed restored NADPH oxidase immune activity within one month, sustained through 4-6 months of follow-up, with no clinically significant treatment-related adverse events.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the NEJM site directly on 2026-07-25: no retraction or correction found.

title: A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing
summary: Using the newly completed FlyWire connectome (125,000+ neurons, ~50 million synapses) of the adult Drosophila central brain, Shiu, Sterne, Scott and colleagues built a leaky integrate-and-fire model that treats each neuron as a simple threshold unit wired according to measured synaptic connectivity and predicted neurotransmitter identity. Across 164 experimentally testable predictions about which neurons activate downstream of specific taste, water, or mechanosensory inputs, the model matched optogenetic and behavioral validation about 91% of the time, including circuits for feeding initiation and grooming sequences. It's a deliberately simple model — no neuromodulation, no spontaneous/basal firing, no learning — so it's best read as evidence that synapse-level wiring diagrams plus coarse dynamics already predict a surprising amount of circuit behavior, not as a full simulation of a working brain.
retraction_status: none found — checked Retraction Watch (no hits for search terms) and general PubPeer-targeted search (no discussion page found); no correction/erratum listed on the Nature article page as of 2026-07-25

title: Decisional reference point pathology: a cognitive mechanism for and a correlate of major depressive disorder in humans
summary: Vittala, Glimcher and colleagues at NYU test whether major depressive disorder involves a miscalibrated 'decisional reference point' — the internal benchmark against which outcomes are judged good or bad — using a foraging task and a bidding task in 50 MDD patients versus 70 controls. Depressed patients showed reference points elevated roughly 50% above controls, the elevation tracked symptom severity (r=0.71), and patients were specifically impaired at updating the reference point when conditions changed, not simply stuck at a fixed high baseline. The authors propose a roughly three-minute behavioral task as a possible objective severity marker; this is a cross-sectional behavioral-economics study, not an intervention trial, so causality and generalizability beyond this sample remain open questions.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
retraction_status: none found — checked Retraction Watch (no hits) and general search for corrections/PubPeer activity; paper is very recent (May 2026) so absence of scrutiny is expected rather than reassuring

title: Innovations in noninvasive sensory stimulation treatments to combat Alzheimer's disease
summary: This is a synthesis essay, not new experimental data — Park and Tsai (MIT Picower Institute) survey a decade of work on 40Hz sensory 'GENUS' stimulation (flickering light/sound), covering mouse-model reductions in amyloid/tau and improved cognition/behavior, plus proposed mechanisms (microglial state shifts, vascular clearance, oscillatory entrainment). It's worth reading alongside the field's real replication problems: a 2023 Nature Neuroscience study from the Buzsáki lab found 40Hz light stimulation failed to entrain native gamma oscillations in an AD mouse model, so the entrainment mechanism itself is contested even as human trials proceed. Useful primer on where the clinical evidence stands, but it's an advocacy-adjacent review from a lab with a direct stake in GENUS, not neutral arbitration of the controversy.
retraction_status: none found — checked Retraction Watch and PubPeer-targeted search, no results

title: A Chemically Defined Synthetic Cell Capable Of Growth And Replication
summary: SpudCell, from Katarzyna Adamala's group (soon housed at the new nonprofit Biotic), is a from-scratch synthetic cell built entirely from purified, non-living parts rather than pared down from an existing organism — carrying a 90 kb genome across several DNA molecules that support transcription, translation, genome replication, membrane growth via fusion with feeder liposomes, and division. In a five-generation competition assay, a mutant lineage overproducing alpha-hemolysin (linked to mechanical division) outcompeted the standard line — a small but real demonstration of heritable selection. Caveats matter: the cell can't make its own ribosomes or ATP and depends on constant external feeding, genome segregation is unreliable (~33% of daughters retain the full genome set by generation five), and the manuscript — posted to bioRxiv after reportedly being turned down by Cell, with one reviewer calling it 'not real biology' — has not yet cleared formal peer review. Adamala herself says plainly that 'this cell is not alive by any definition.'
journal: bioRxiv (preprint, not yet peer-reviewed at a journal)
retraction_status: none found (it's a preprint, so 'retraction' doesn't strictly apply); no corrections noted on bioRxiv; not indexed on Retraction Watch or PubPeer as of 2026-07-25

title: Confronting risks of mirror life
summary: This is a consensus risk-assessment piece, not an experimental paper: 38 authors (including Adamala, Church, Szostak, Venter, and others) summarize a roughly 300-page technical report arguing that mirror bacteria — built from mirror-image nucleic acids and proteins — would likely evade both innate immunity and much of the antibiotic/predator ecosystem that has coevolved around normal chirality, and that although the capability is probably a decade-plus away, it's close enough to warrant preemptive restriction now. It reads as unusually decisive for a consensus statement (several signatories reportedly started more skeptical of the risk and moved toward concern after reviewing the modeling), though public commentary from some researchers has pushed back on the timeline and worst-case severity estimates rather than the core chirality-evasion logic.
retraction_status: none found — checked Retraction Watch (no hits) and PubPeer-targeted search, no discussion found

title: Stem Cell-Derived, Fully Differentiated Islets for Type 1 Diabetes
summary: Vertex's allogeneic, fully differentiated stem-cell-derived islet cell therapy (zimislecel, formerly VX-880) is infused into the hepatic portal vein under chronic immunosuppression. In this NEJM report of 12 patients followed at least a year, all showed restored glucose-responsive endogenous insulin secretion and elimination of severe hypoglycemic events, with 11 of 12 reaching reduced or zero exogenous insulin need. Unlike encapsulated-cell approaches, these are 'naked' islets requiring standard immunosuppression, restricting eligibility to patients with severe hypoglycemia unawareness. Two on-study deaths occurred but were adjudicated as unrelated to the therapy.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found (checked NEJM site, Retraction Watch database, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25).

title: GD2-CAR T cell therapy for H3K27M-mutated diffuse midline gliomas
summary: A phase 1 dose-escalation trial delivering GD2-directed CAR T cells intravenously (and later intracerebroventricularly) to children and young adults with H3K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma, including DIPG — a nearly uniformly fatal brainstem tumor. Three of the first four patients showed clinical and radiographic improvement, establishing proof-of-concept that CAR T cells can act against a solid CNS tumor via a lineage surface antigen (GD2) rather than the hematologic markers CAR T was originally designed around. Tumor-inflammation-associated neurotoxicity (TIAN) emerged as an expected, manageable on-target side effect.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found for this 2022 paper. Note: a related but distinct 2024 Nature follow-up paper by an overlapping author group ("Intravenous and intracranial GD2-CAR T cells for H3K27M+ diffuse midline gliomas," s41586-024-08171-9) did receive an Author Correction in Nov. 2024 — that correction applies to the 2024 paper, not this 2022 one.

title: Combined Whole Eye and Face Transplant: Microsurgical Strategy and 1-Year Clinical Course
summary: First published report of a combined whole-eye and face allotransplant in a human, describing the microsurgical strategy and 1-year outcomes for a patient who lost his left eye and much of his face in a high-voltage electrical accident. The transplanted eye maintained normal intraocular pressure and blood flow (unlike animal models, where transplanted eyes typically shrink) and showed electroretinographic photoreceptor responses to light, but there was no restored conscious visual perception at 1 year. Notable methodologically for the first intraoperative injection of stem cells into a human optic nerve to attempt to promote regeneration.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found (checked JAMA site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25).

title: Molecular basis of positional memory in limb regeneration
summary: Identifies a Hand2-Shh positive-feedback loop that encodes posterior positional identity in the axolotl limb — established during development, retained into adulthood as 'positional memory,' and reactivated after amputation to correctly pattern the regenerating blastema. The authors show this circuit can be experimentally rewired to convert anterior cells into posterior identity, directly addressing how regeneration-competent tissue 'remembers' its original position, a mechanistic question central to efforts translating regenerative capacity toward non-regenerating species (including mammals).
retraction_status: no retraction or correction found (checked Nature site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25)

title: Donanemab in Early Symptomatic Alzheimer Disease: The TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 Randomized Clinical Trial
summary: Phase 3 trial (n=1736) of the anti-amyloid antibody donanemab in early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease, showing roughly a 35% (low/medium tau subgroup) to 22% (combined population) slowing of clinical and functional decline over 18 months versus placebo. Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (brain swelling in ~24%, microbleeds in ~31%) occurred at meaningfully higher rates than placebo, including deaths attributed to ARIA. One of the two pivotal trials (with lecanemab's Clarity AD) underpinning current amyloid-antibody approvals, though the modest absolute effect size keeps the clinical relevance of amyloid clearance actively contested.
retraction_status: No retraction found. Not aware of any correction beyond a published author reply to a reader letter, which is normal post-publication discussion, not an erratum (checked JAMA site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25).

title: CD19 CAR T-Cell Therapy in Autoimmune Disease — A Case Series with Follow-up
summary: Case series of 15 patients with severe, treatment-refractory SLE, idiopathic inflammatory myositis, or systemic sclerosis given a single CD19 CAR T-cell infusion after fludarabine/cyclophosphamide lymphodepletion. Patients achieved drug-free remission with deep B-cell depletion and re-emergence of a naive B-cell repertoire on reconstitution, without severe CRS or neurotoxicity — the paper that launched CD19 CAR-T as an autoimmune-disease 'immune reset' strategy, distinct from its origin treating B-cell malignancies. A subsequent case report showed relapse and CAR-directed immune rejection on re-treatment in one patient, underscoring that durability is not guaranteed for everyone.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found (checked NEJM site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25).

title: Whole-brain annotation and multi-connectome cell typing of Drosophila
summary: Companion paper to the FlyWire whole-brain connectome, providing systematic, hierarchical annotation of all ~139,000 neurons of the adult female Drosophila brain into cell types and developmental hemilineages (8,453 cell types total, over half newly described), unifying it with the earlier partial hemibrain dataset. Supplies the human-readable 'parts list' needed to computationally query or simulate the fly brain; since roughly 75% of human disease-associated genes have fly homologs, it's a reference point for circuit-level modeling of neurological disease mechanisms.
retraction_status: no retraction or correction found (checked Nature site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25)

title: Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain
summary: Single-nucleus RNA-sequencing atlas sampling over 3 million nuclei across roughly 100 dissections spanning the entire adult human brain (forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain) from three postmortem donors, identifying 461 clusters and 3,313 subclusters organized largely by developmental origin, with markedly higher cell-type diversity in midbrain/hindbrain neurons than cortex. Functions as the transcriptomic reference companion to spatial and connectomic brain atlases — useful groundwork for anchoring circuit-level or disease-focused neuroscience to defined molecular cell types.
retraction_status: no retraction or correction found (checked Science site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25)

title: Accurate structure prediction of biomolecular interactions with AlphaFold 3
summary: Diffusion-based successor to AlphaFold2 that jointly predicts structures of proteins in complex with nucleic acids, small-molecule ligands, ions, and chemically modified residues, substantially outperforming specialized docking and nucleic-acid-specific prediction tools on internal benchmarks. Independent third-party benchmarking published since found the accuracy advantage shrinks markedly for structures released after AlphaFold3's training cutoff and for chemically dissimilar ligands, suggesting part of the reported improvement reflects training-data memorization rather than pure generalization — a caveat worth flagging given how heavily the tool is now used in drug discovery pipelines.
retraction_status: No retraction. An Addendum was published (Nature 636, E4, Nov. 2024) correcting pseudocode in the Supplementary Information; this is a correction to supplementary methods documentation, not a retraction (checked Nature site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25).

title: Simulating 500 million years of evolution with a language model
summary: Introduces ESM3, a generative multimodal protein language model (up to 98 billion parameters, trained on ~2.8 billion natural protein sequences) that jointly reasons over sequence, structure, and function. Prompted to design a novel fluorescent protein, ESM3 generated a bright GFP variant only 58% sequence-identical to any known natural fluorescent protein — a jump the authors estimate is equivalent to roughly 500 million years of natural evolutionary divergence. Demonstrates that language models can be steered to explore functional protein space well beyond what evolution has actually sampled, though independent reviewers note zero-shot performance is inconsistent for highly divergent protein families and model confidence doesn't always track correctness.
retraction_status: no retraction or correction found (checked Science site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25)

title: Millimetre-scale bioresorbable optoelectronic systems for electrotherapy
summary: A grain-of-rice-sized, fully bioresorbable, wirelessly light-activated pacemaker (1.8 x 3.5 x 1 mm) paired with a soft skin-mounted sensor that autonomously fires a light pulse to trigger pacing when it detects a dangerously slow heart rate, then dissolves harmlessly in the body once no longer needed — e.g., during recovery from cardiac surgery. Eliminates the second surgery normally required to remove a temporary pacing wire, and at more than 20x smaller than the group's own prior bioresorbable pacing device, extends this Rogers-lab bioelectronics platform toward broader electrotherapy applications (nerve/bone healing, wound treatment, pain blocking).
retraction_status: no retraction or correction found (checked Nature site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25)

title: Chronic adaptive deep brain stimulation versus conventional stimulation in Parkinson's disease: a blinded randomized feasibility trial
summary: Blinded, randomized crossover feasibility trial in four Parkinson's patients comparing brain-sensing 'adaptive' DBS — which adjusts stimulation intensity in real time based on subthalamic/cortical gamma oscillations that track dopaminergic state — against continuous conventional DBS. Adaptive stimulation better controlled motor fluctuations and improved quality of life relative to conventional stimulation. The tiny sample size (n=4) limits generalizability, but this is the proof-of-concept precursor to the larger multi-site adaptive-DBS trials now underway testing closed-loop neuromodulation as a deployable clinical product rather than a research prototype.
retraction_status: no retraction or correction found (checked Nature site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25)

title: Incorporation of hair follicles in 3D bioprinted models of human skin
summary: 3D-bioprints dermal papilla cells and endothelial cells within a fibroblast-laden dermal matrix to nucleate hair-follicle-like structures inside lab-grown human skin constructs, addressing a long-standing gap in tissue-engineered skin: current grafts cover a wound but lack adnexal structures (hair, and eventually sweat/sebaceous glands) needed for fully functional skin replacement. This is proof-of-concept in vitro work — functional hair growth, vascular integration, and in vivo performance in an actual wound remain to be demonstrated.
retraction_status: no retraction or correction found (checked Science Advances site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25)

title: Systematic production of human kidney organoids for transplantation in porcine kidneys during ex vivo machine perfusion
summary: Establishes a scalable, reproducible protocol for producing human pluripotent stem-cell-derived kidney organoids containing nephron-like proximal/distal tubule and glomerular structures, then infuses them into ex vivo porcine kidneys during normothermic machine perfusion. The organoids integrated into porcine renal tissue, stayed viable, and did not trigger acute immune rejection through 48 hours post-transplant, with the host kidney continuing to function normally — a step toward using machine-perfused donor organs as a 'bioreactor' host for growing and testing human replacement tissue, as an alternative to interspecies chimeras or synthetic scaffolds.
retraction_status: no retraction or correction found (checked Nature site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25)

title: CRISPR-Cas9 In Vivo Gene Editing for Transthyretin Amyloidosis
summary: First systemic (intravenous) CRISPR-Cas9 in vivo gene-editing therapy tested in humans: a lipid-nanoparticle-delivered Cas9 mRNA plus guide RNA (NTLA-2001) that knocks out the TTR gene in hepatocytes to treat hereditary transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis. In this 6-patient dose-escalation cohort, treatment produced dose-dependent, substantial reductions in serum TTR with only mild adverse events. Distinct from RNA-interference competitors (patisiran, vutrisiran) in offering a single-dose, permanent genomic edit rather than a repeat-dosed knockdown — trading the durability of a one-time fix against the irreversibility of permanently altering the genome.
retraction_status: no retraction or correction found (checked NEJM site, Retraction Watch, PubPeer as of 2026-07-25)

title: GPNMB-directed CAR T cell therapy against MiT/TFE-family fusion-driven solid tumors
summary: Researchers identified glycoprotein NMB (GPNMB) as a highly and stably expressed target on MiT/TFE-family fusion-driven cancers, including alveolar soft-part sarcoma and translocation renal cell carcinoma, and engineered GCAR1, a CAR T-cell product against it. GCAR1 showed potent activity in patient-matched cells, organoids, and xenograft models, and in a first-in-human trial produced disease stabilization and shrinkage of non-target lesions in a patient with metastatic, treatment-refractory sarcoma, with good tolerability. The work offers a rare proof-of-concept for CAR-T efficacy against solid tumors, historically a major weak point for cellular immunotherapy.
retraction_status: No retraction, correction, or PubPeer flags found as of 2026-07-27 (checked journal site, PubMed, and PubPeer).

title: Magnetoelectric microrobots for spinal cord injury regeneration
summary: Researchers at ETH Zurich and the University of Zurich built microscopic biohybrid robots, dubbed NPCbots, by fusing human iPSC-derived neural progenitor cells with magnetoelectric nanoparticles that can be wirelessly steered to an injury site and electrically stimulated using an external magnetic field. In zebrafish with spinal cord injuries, magnetically stimulated NPCbots drove rapid neuronal and glial differentiation and restored near-normal swimming within three days; in mice with fully severed spinal cords, treated animals showed reconnected nerve fibers and markedly improved gait and coordination after 28 days. The approach offers a minimally invasive way to both deliver and precisely activate regenerative stem cells at an injury site without genetic modification.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found. Checked Retraction Watch and PubPeer on 2026-07-27; no entries for this paper or its authors.

title: Teclistamab in Multiple Myeloma with One to Three Previous Lines of Therapy
summary: In the international phase 3 MajesTEC-9 trial, 593 patients with relapsed multiple myeloma (after 1-3 prior treatments) were randomized to the bispecific T-cell-engaging antibody teclistamab alone versus standard triplet chemo-immunotherapy regimens. Teclistamab monotherapy cut the risk of death by 40% and the risk of progression or death by 71%, with 18-month overall survival of 79.2% versus 68.6% and complete-response rates of 66% versus 17% for standard care. The results suggest bispecific antibodies could replace older combination regimens as early as first relapse in myeloma, a notable finding given that survival benefits are uncommon in myeloma trials at this stage of disease.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found. Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the NEJM article page directly on 2026-07-27; no notices identified.

title: Dyscoordination of thalamic reticular spindles is associated with social memory deficits in mice and humans with autism spectrum disorder
summary: Researchers pinpointed a specific thalamic circuit -- parvalbumin neurons in the sensory thalamic reticular nucleus projecting to the visual thalamus -- that generates the sleep spindles needed to consolidate social memories overnight. In a mouse model of autism (Neuroligin-2 mutants), boosting activity in this circuit with optogenetics restored normal spindles and rescued social memory deficits, while in children, spindle characteristics measured by EEG could be fed into a machine-learning model to help flag autism spectrum disorder. The work links a concrete sleep-circuit mechanism to a hallmark of autism and points toward sleep-based diagnostics and possible circuit-targeted interventions.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found as of 2026-07-27. Checked Retraction Watch and PubPeer for the DOI, authors, and title -- no entries found. Paper was published online 2026-07-23 with no flags on the Nature Communications article page.

title: A wireless subdural-contained brain-computer interface with 65,536 electrodes and 1,024 channels
summary: Researchers at Columbia, Stanford, Penn, and NewYork-Presbyterian built BISC, a single hair-thin CMOS chip that packs 65,536 recording electrodes, 1,024 simultaneous recording channels, and 16,384 stimulation channels into a device under 3 cubic millimeters -- over 1,000 times smaller than comparable brain implants. The chip sits on the brain's surface (subdural, non-penetrating) and wirelessly streams data at 100 Mbps, roughly 100 times faster than prior wireless brain-computer interfaces. The team validated the device with chronic recordings in animal motor and visual cortex and has begun short-term intraoperative recordings in humans, aiming toward future use in speech, motor, and vision restoration for paralysis, ALS, and blindness.
retraction_status: No retraction, correction, or expression of concern found. Checked the journal site, Retraction Watch, and PubPeer as of 2026-07-27 -- none found.

title: Patterning human kidney organoids with synthetic Wnt-secreting organizers
summary: Researchers mapped a previously unrecognized WNT11/WNT9B signaling boundary that organizes nephron formation in the developing human kidney, then engineered synthetic 'organizer' cells that secrete tunable amounts of WNT protein inside stem-cell-derived kidney organoids. These synthetic organizers restored the missing spatial cue, driving reproducible, correctly oriented nephron patterning along the proximal-distal axis where organoids previously self-organized chaotically. The approach, validated with single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, offers a synthetic-biology blueprint for making organoids more faithful models of real organs and a step toward engineering transplantable kidney tissue.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found. Checked the journal site, Retraction Watch, and PubPeer on 2026-07-27; no records of retraction, correction, or post-publication concerns.

title: Ciltacabtagene autoleucel in high-risk smoldering multiple myeloma: the CAR-PRISM phase 2 trial
summary: In the first prospective trial of CAR T-cell therapy for a precursor cancer condition, Dana-Farber researchers gave a single infusion of the BCMA-directed CAR-T product ciltacabtagene autoleucel to 20 patients with high-risk smoldering multiple myeloma, before the disease had progressed to symptomatic cancer. All 20 patients achieved undetectable minimal residual disease, and remissions were sustained through a median follow-up of 15.3 months with no progression to active myeloma, though most patients had transient high-grade cytopenias and all had low-grade cytokine release syndrome. The results raise the provocative possibility of intercepting myeloma before it becomes an active malignancy, while reopening debate about using an aggressive, toxicity-prone therapy in patients who do not yet have cancer.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the Nature Medicine journal site on 2026-07-31 for this paper (CAR-PRISM trial, ciltacabtagene autoleucel in smoldering myeloma) and its authors; no retraction or correction notices found.

title: An iPSC-derived neural progenitor cell therapy for subacute spinal cord injury: a phase 1 trial with long-term follow-up
summary: Researchers at Keio University led by Hideyuki Okano and Masaya Nakamura report the world's first human transplantation of induced-pluripotent-stem-cell-derived neural stem/progenitor cells into the spinal cord, in four patients with subacute complete cervical spinal cord injury. Over 2-4 years of follow-up with MRI and standardized neurological assessments, the therapy met its primary safety endpoint with no tumor formation or graft-related serious adverse events, while exploratory results showed a median 13-point improvement in motor score and ASIA/AIS grade conversion in two of the four patients. The study establishes long-term feasibility and safety of an iPSC-derived cell therapy for a historically difficult-to-treat form of nerve tissue damage.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the Nature Medicine journal site on 2026-07-31 for this paper and the broader Okano/Nakamura iPSC-NS/PC spinal-cord-injury research program; no retraction or correction notices found.

title: Phase 3 Trial of Weekly Oral Islatravir-Lenacapavir for HIV-1 Treatment
summary: In the ISLEND-1 phase 3 trial, 607 adults with virologically suppressed HIV-1 were randomized to switch to a once-weekly single-tablet regimen of oral islatravir-lenacapavir or to continue their daily bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide regimen. At week 48, the weekly regimen was noninferior to the daily standard of care (0% vs 0.3% with HIV-1 RNA >=50 copies/mL; suppression maintained in 93.4% vs 92.4%), with a similar safety profile and no new safety signals. If confirmed and approved, this would be the first oral HIV treatment patients take only once a week instead of daily, a potentially major convenience and adherence advance.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch and the NEJM article page on 2026-07-31 for this paper and the ISLEND-1/ISLEND-2 trial program; no retraction or correction notices found.

title: Mapping the neuronal building blocks of human language with language models
summary: Using microelectrode arrays implanted in eight epilepsy patients, researchers recorded 579 individual neurons across the frontal and temporal lobes while participants spoke naturally, producing thousands of words across natural conversation. Pairing these single-neuron recordings with natural-language-processing models, the team found that language is not localized to one grammar center but is encoded by scattered, specialized neuron populations: some track parts of speech, others track hierarchical sentence structure or word-to-word dependencies, and a small subset integrates both grammar and meaning simultaneously. The work offers one of the most fine-grained pictures yet of how the human brain builds sentences at the cellular level.
retraction_status: Checked Retraction Watch, PubPeer, and the Nature journal page on 2026-07-31 for this paper; no retraction or correction notices found.

title: CD19 CAR-T cells for treatment-refractory autoimmune diseases: the phase 1/2 CASTLE basket trial
summary: In this phase 1/2 basket trial, researchers gave a single infusion of autologous CD19-directed CAR T cells (zorpocabtagene autoleucel) to 24 patients with severe, treatment-resistant systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, or idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, most of whom had failed a median of four prior immunosuppressive regimens. The therapy avoided high-grade cytokine release syndrome or neurotoxicity, and the majority of patients achieved disease remission or stabilization while living free of steroids and other immunosuppressants for more than six months. It is one of the largest and most rigorous demonstrations yet that a single 'immune reset' with CAR T cells can durably control multiple distinct autoimmune diseases rather than just cancer.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found. Checked Retraction Watch database, PubPeer, and the Nature Medicine article page directly (s41591-025-04185-6) as of 2026-08-02; no retraction, expression of concern, or correction notices identified.

title: Genetically engineered pig-to-human liver xenotransplantation
summary: Surgeons in China transplanted an auxiliary liver from a pig carrying ten genetic edits into a 71-year-old man with hepatitis B-related cirrhosis and a hepatocellular carcinoma that made standard resection or human liver transplantation impossible. The xenograft immediately produced bile and synthesized clotting factors and albumin with no hyperacute rejection, functioning for over a month before a thrombotic complication led to its removal on day 38; the patient survived 171 days total. It is the first detailed report of a genetically engineered pig liver sustaining measurable synthetic function in a living human, offering proof of concept for xenotransplantation as a bridge therapy for liver failure.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found. Checked Retraction Watch database, PubPeer, and the Journal of Hepatology site directly as of 2026-08-02; none found. The paper prompted two published critical letters (on thrombotic-microangiopathy-vs-rejection interpretation and on remaining translational barriers) with an authors' reply -- normal post-publication scientific discourse, not a correction or retraction.

title: Enfortumab Vedotin and Pembrolizumab in Cisplatin-Eligible Bladder Cancer
summary: In this international phase 3 trial (KEYNOTE-B15/EV-304), 808 patients with cisplatin-eligible muscle-invasive bladder cancer were randomized to perioperative enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab or standard neoadjuvant cisplatin-gemcitabine chemotherapy before and after radical cystectomy. The antibody-drug conjugate/immunotherapy combination nearly doubled the rate of pathological complete response (55.8% vs 32.5%) and significantly improved event-free and overall survival, at the cost of somewhat higher grade 3+ adverse events. The results, the first regimen in nearly 25 years to surpass the long-standing chemotherapy standard, led the FDA to expand approval of enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab to all cisplatin-eligible cystectomy candidates in July 2026.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found. Checked the NEJM article page, Retraction Watch database, and PubPeer as of 2026-08-02; no notices, expressions of concern, or corrections identified for this article (published July 23, 2026).

title: Representations of the intrinsic value of information in mouse orbitofrontal cortex
summary: Using an odor-cued information-seeking task and single-cell calcium imaging, researchers show that mice will sacrifice water reward just to learn information that has no effect on the outcome, revealing that curiosity itself has measurable value to the brain. Neurons in the orbitofrontal cortex encode this 'value of information' through a population distinct from the neurons that track ordinary reward value, with a computational latent-variable model confirming the two signals follow separate pathways. The work gives one of the clearest neural mechanisms yet for curiosity-driven, non-instrumental information seeking, a behavior long observed but poorly understood at the circuit level.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found. Checked Retraction Watch database, PubPeer, and the Nature Neuroscience article page directly; no corrections, expressions of concern, or retractions on record for this paper or its long-running bioRxiv preprint (posted 2023, revised through 2024).

title: In vivo CAR T cell generation to treat cancer and autoimmune disease
summary: Researchers at Capstan Therapeutics and collaborators engineered targeted lipid nanoparticles (tLNPs) that deliver CAR-encoding mRNA directly to T cells inside the body, reprogramming them into CAR T cells without the need for leukapheresis, ex vivo manufacturing, or lymphodepleting chemotherapy. The tLNPs controlled tumors in humanized mice and produced durable B-cell depletion with naive B-cell reconstitution in cynomolgus monkeys, suggesting a path to reset autoimmune-driven immune responses. This off-the-shelf, in-body approach could dramatically simplify and broaden access to CAR T therapy for both cancer and autoimmune disease, and the underlying platform was significant enough to drive AbbVie's $2.1 billion acquisition of Capstan Therapeutics.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found. Checked Retraction Watch database (no results), PubPeer (no entries found), and the Science journal site (no correction notice) as of 2026-08-04.

title: Reversing lysosomal dysfunction restores youthful state in aged hematopoietic stem cells
summary: Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai found that aged blood-forming (hematopoietic) stem cells in mice accumulate hyperactive, damaged lysosomes that drive metabolic, epigenetic, and inflammatory dysfunction. Briefly treating old stem cells with a vacuolar ATPase inhibitor to calm this lysosomal overactivity restored their youthful molecular state and boosted their blood-regenerating capacity more than eightfold after transplantation. The work challenges the assumption that stem-cell aging is irreversible and points to lysosomal function as a druggable target for rejuvenating the blood and immune system in older age.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found. Checked Retraction Watch database, PubPeer, and the Cell Press/Cell Stem Cell journal site (as of 2026-08-04) — no records of any retraction, correction, or post-publication concern for this article.

title: Assessment of adverse effects attributed to statin therapy in product labels: a meta-analysis of double-blind randomised controlled trials
summary: An international team, the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' (CTT) Collaboration, pooled individual-patient data from 19 double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trials of statins (nearly 124,000 participants) to test whether the dozens of side effects listed on statin drug labels are actually caused by the drugs. Only 4 of 66 labeled adverse effects — abnormal liver enzymes, other liver test abnormalities, urinary composition changes, and edema — occurred significantly more often with statins than placebo; widely feared effects such as muscle pain, memory loss, depression, fatigue, and erectile dysfunction showed no excess risk when assessed under blinded trial conditions. The findings suggest that statin product labeling, largely derived from unblinded observational reports, substantially overstates the drugs' harms and could reshape prescribing guidance and patient counseling for one of the most widely used drug classes in the world.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found. Checked Retraction Watch (lancet category listing), PubPeer, and The Lancet's own site/Department of Error notices as of 2026-08-04 — none reference this article. A standard post-publication scientific correspondence was published (a critical letter and the authors' reply, 'Challenges in assessing statin-associated adverse events'), which is normal scientific debate, not a correction or retraction.

title: Real-time brain-controlled selective hearing enhances speech perception in multi-talker environments
summary: Researchers at Columbia, Cornell and NYU built a closed-loop brain-computer interface that reads intracranial EEG signals from neurosurgical patients to figure out, in real time, which of several simultaneous talkers a listener is attending to, then automatically boosts that voice's volume. In multiple experiments the system decoded attention with 72-90% accuracy, improved speech intelligibility, reduced listening effort, tracked spontaneous shifts of attention, and was consistently preferred by participants over unamplified listening. It is presented as a first proof-of-concept for a future generation of 'neuro-steered' hearing aids that solve the classic cocktail-party problem by using the brain itself as the control signal.
retraction_status: No retraction or correction found.
